lesson.title: What Actually Stops a Population from Growing
lesson.summary: Limiting factors are the specific resources or conditions, such as food, water, light, or space, that restrict how large a population can grow, and they are what give carrying capacity its particular value in a particular place.
lesson.body:
Carrying capacity is a useful number, but it does not explain itself. Asking why a pond can only support so many fish, or why a meadow can only support so many rabbits, leads directly to the idea of a limiting factor: whatever resource or condition is in short enough supply that it caps population growth before anything else does.

A long standing idea in ecology, sometimes called the law of the minimum, holds that population growth is constrained not by the total pool of resources available but specifically by whichever resource is scarcest relative to what the population needs. A desert plant population might have plenty of sunlight and nutrients but still be capped by water availability. A lake's algae might have abundant sunlight and nitrogen but be capped by a scarce nutrient like phosphorus. Whatever the scarcest necessity is, that is the limiting factor, and adding more of everything else will not raise the population until that one constraint eases.

It is useful to sort limiting factors into two broad categories. Abiotic limiting factors are nonliving: temperature, water availability, light, soil nutrients, physical space, pH, salinity. Biotic limiting factors involve other living things: food availability, predators, disease causing organisms, and competitors. Both categories can set the ceiling on a population, and which one matters most typically depends on the species and the habitat. A population of barnacles on a rocky shore might be limited mainly by available space to attach to, an abiotic and structural factor, while a population of rabbits in a grassy field might be limited mainly by predation pressure, a biotic factor.

This same logic shows up directly in agriculture, where farmers have long known that adding more of a nutrient that is already abundant in the soil does nothing for crop yield if a different nutrient, often nitrogen or phosphorus, is the one running short. Whatever nutrient is scarcest sets the ceiling on how much the crop can grow, no matter how much of everything else is supplied.

It is also worth noting that limiting factors do not always act with the same strength regardless of how many individuals are present. Some, like a sudden freeze, tend to hit a population about as hard whether it is large or small. Others, like competition for food or the spread of disease, get more intense specifically because a population has grown crowded. That distinction, between factors that scale with density and those that do not, is exactly what the next two chapters explore.
